Q: Best way to handle OAuth + JWT emitted by backend? A:

I had a similar situation (but with a mobile app) and opted to go for something akin to the 3rd option. In my case, the mobile app calls a backend endpoint and provides the callback URL. The backend endpoint prepares the appropriate redirect to the 3rd party auth provider and passes its own callback URL to that. After signing in via the OAuth provider the backend callback endpoint is called which can then persist some user information if needed and the backend callback endpoint then redirects to the callback that the mobile app had provided previously.

Here are the pros and cons of this and why we chose to do this:

Pros

  1. We can create a new user in our backend database if needed before redirect back to the app. The app benefits from having a user that is pre-popuated with some sensible defaults without needing an additional round-trip to set them
  2. The backend can handle changes to the 3rd party sign-in API. In our case this is an advantage because publishing a new version of the app has to go through appstore/playstore review processes which may take time and signing in will be broken in the meantime.
  3. We can potentially use the same backend for the mobile app and other apps that consume the backend without code duplication (we don't currently but a webapp is being planned)

Cons

  1. It need a degree of trust required: Users may trust the 3rd party sign in provider so would not mind being redirected directly to that but may be more sceptical if they have to go through another endpoint they may not recognise. Again we own the backend and it's under a domain users recognise so it is not a problem for us
  2. It makes the backend endpoint harder to update because the app relies on and and we'd need to release a new version of the app if we were to do that
  3. It is susceptible to code issues on our end rather than on code issues on a (possibly) better tested and scrutinised service (we're the only ones that use our backend but the 3rd party OAuth provider is more widely used so issues are discovered and fixed faster).

I don't necessarily suggest you should do this. What I am going to suggest is to weigh pros and cons based on your specific situation and determine what works better for security and maintainability.

Q: How to make jansi work in a jpackage image on windows A:

Support for the JAnsi library was removed in Log4j Core 2.25.0 (see release notes). The rationale is that ANSI escape support in the Windows 10 console has been around for almost a decade (since 2017) and can be enabled by setting the registry key:

HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Console\VirtualTerminalLevel

to 0x1. See ANSI Styling on Windows for more details.

Note: even previous versions never supported JAnsi 2.x (see issue #1736).

Q: Magento Google tag manager manually A:

Yes, you can integrate Google Tag Manager manually in Magento, but you need to consider how Magento rendering and caching work.

The basic setup usually includes:

1. Add GTM script to the <head> and <body>
You can do this via:

Custom module
Theme layout XML
Admin → Content → Configuration → HTML Head

For example, in layout XML:

<head>
<script>
// GTM head script
</script>
</head>

And the <noscript> part in the body container.

2. Push Magento data to the dataLayer

The biggest challenge is not GTM installation but sending correct data. Magento does not expose product, cart, or order data automatically, so you must inject it manually.

Example on the product page:

<script>
window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
dataLayer.push({
event: 'view_item',
ecommerce: {
items: [{
item_id: '<?= $_product->getSku() ?>',
item_name: '<?= $_product->getName() ?>'
}]
}
});
</script>

3. Handle dynamic checkout

Magento 2 checkout is Knockout‑based, so standard template tracking won’t work. You need to subscribe to JS components or override checkout modules.

This is why manual GTM integration often becomes difficult to maintain, especially when upgrading Magento or switching themes.

Because of that, many developers use ready modules that already handle:

Checkout tracking
Enhanced Ecommerce
GA4
Dynamic events
AJAX reloads
Compatibility with Magento updates

For example, the Magefan google tag manager extesnion for Magento can be useful as a reference implementation, even if your goal is a custom setup.

So manual integration is possible, but make sure to architect it as a module and not a quick template injection. Otherwise, you will likely face tracking issues later.
